# HTTP GET vs. HEAD

**Release:** `AUDIT_RESEARCH_CURRENT`  
**Audience:** Software team

## Concise comparison

| Aspect | GET | HEAD |
|---|---|---|
| Intent | Requests transfer of a representation of the target resource. | Has the same semantics as GET, except the server **MUST NOT** send content in the response. |
| Response data | Delivers the representation when the response carries content. | Carries no response content; it is for obtaining metadata without transferring the representation data. |
| Headers/metadata | Supplies the response fields associated with the selected representation. | The server **SHOULD** send the same header fields as it would for GET, but **MAY** omit fields whose values are determined only while generating content. Therefore, clients should not require byte-for-byte header identity. |
| Method properties | Safe and idempotent. | Safe and idempotent. |

## Engineering guidance

Use GET when the client needs the representation. Use HEAD when it needs metadata—for example, to check a link or determine whether a representation changed—while avoiding representation transfer. Treat HEAD as a metadata-only request for the same selected representation, but allow the documented header omissions. HTTP caching also defines a HEAD response as equivalent to the corresponding GET response without content; it can be used to invalidate or update a cached GET response in specified cases.

## Sources (primary)

1. IETF, **RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics**, §§9.3.1–9.3.2 and §18.2:  
   GET: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.1  
   HEAD: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.2  
   Method properties: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-18.2
2. IETF, **RFC 9111: HTTP Caching**, §4.3.5:  
   https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-4.3.5

The report is based on two primary sources; no secondary source was used as evidence.
